summary: This interview transcript, featuring an STS postdoctoral researcher, strongly exemplifies Reflexivity and Public Engagement, alongside a critical assessment of the lack of Responsiveness. The respondent demonstrates epistemic humility and self-scrutiny regarding their own research origins and the hidden biases of traffic optimisation models. Engagement is robustly framed through an inclusive, participant-led advisory group where non-expert stakeholders set the agenda. However, the account highlights a stark deficit in Responsiveness: despite meaningful engagement and warm receptions from authorities, there are no institutional mechanisms to translate citizen input into actual parameter changes, resulting in participation washing without trajectory adaptation. Anticipation is absent from this excerpt, as the focus centers on critiquing current design logic and governance failures rather than exploring long-term scenarios or alternative futures.
transcript:
Interview transcript A02 — Postdoctoral researcher, science and technology studies
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] How did you come to study this deployment?
[Respondent] I was going to study something else entirely and then I moved to Port Calder and started noticing that the junction outside my flat behaved differently on different days. That's an embarrassing origin story for a research programme but it's the true one. I should say that up front because where a question comes from shapes what you look at, and I was already annoyed before I started.
[Interviewer] What have you found?
[Respondent] The thing I keep coming back to is who gets asked to adapt. The system optimises flow. Flow is measured in vehicles. So when the model has a choice between holding twelve cars and holding one person with a walking frame, the arithmetic is not close. Nobody chose that. It falls out of what got counted.
[Interviewer] Have you worked with residents directly?
[Respondent] Yes, that's most of what I do now. We set up a group with a disability advocacy organisation and a residents' association — eleven people, meeting monthly, and they set the agenda, not me. The first three meetings I talked too much and one of them told me so, which was the most useful supervision I've had.
[Interviewer] Has any of it changed the system?
[Respondent] No. And I want to be careful here because there's a genre of research where the conclusion is 'more participation is needed' and everyone nods and nothing happens. The group has produced two documents. Both were received warmly. Neither changed a parameter. At some point warm reception without change is its own kind of dismissal and I don't yet know what to do about it.
[Interviewer] Is there anything the city does well here?
[Respondent] They answer emails. I'm not being sarcastic — compared with the vendors, the department is reachable and the people in it are thoughtful and underfunded. The problem isn't that they don't care. It's that caring isn't a mechanism. There's no point in the process where what the group says has to be answered in writing before something proceeds. Without that, everything depends on whether the person in post that year happens to be receptive.
